about: Published figures for /luxury-beliefs, each traced to the report that printed it, read through search excerpts on 2026-10-21. Nothing is estimated. Where sources disagree, both are kept. The class breakdowns from the National Family Health Survey are read separately by the scheduled job from the DHS Program's API (nfhs.json).

concept.definition: Ideas and opinions that confer status on the rich at very little cost, while taking a toll on the lower class.
concept.quote: ideas and opinions that confer status on the rich at very little cost, while taking a toll on the lower class (Henderson 2019).

critiques.point: His book loosens the definition: the costs "often", not always, fall on the lower class.
Something in the original definition does not add up — yet the phenomenon is real.

critiques.who: Noah Smith, W. David Marx (as cited)
critiques.point: The label has become an all-purpose epithet for views people dislike.
The causal chains behind the original examples are not supported empirically; the term can dismiss an idea without arguing against it.

areas.belief: Children learn best in their mother tongue, and parents' rush to English-medium schools is a mistake.
areas.whoHolds: Policy: the National Education Policy 2020 recommends the home language as the medium until at least Class 5, and the NCERT director called parents' fascination with English-medium schools "no less than suicide".
areas.whoPays: Families who cannot pass English on at home. Private enrolment keeps rising, though English medium is the stated reason for only a minority of the families who choose it (14% rural, 19.3% urban, NSS 2017-18).

figures.label: Private unaided share of school enrolment, 2023-24
figures.quote: 34.4% for private unaided enrolment and 52.9% for government enrolment in 2023-24

figures.label: Children in private schools whose parents said they were taught in English
figures.quote: Parents of 39% of children in private schools said their children were getting English-medium instruction, but only 10% were actually taught in English.
figures.notes: Azim Premji Foundation: 1,210 families, four states.

figures.label: …who actually were
figures.quote: only 10% were actually taught in English

figures.label: Chose a private school for English medium: rural / urban, 2017-18
figures.quote: about 14% of those who were enrolled in private schools in India's rural areas and 19.3% in urban areas chose a private school because English was the medium of instruction

areas.against: The evidence that early learning in the mother tongue works better is strong, and it is not a status signal; low-fee "English-medium" schools often teach in Hindi or Kannada anyway (57% of children supposed to be in English-medium schools, in the Azim Premji study). Wanting English at Class 6 and the mother tongue to Class 5 are not opposites.
areas.verdict: A real class gap in preference, but the elite position rests on pedagogy, not on status alone.

areas.belief: Chemical fertiliser and genetically modified seed should give way to organic or natural farming.
areas.whoHolds: Activists and some state programmes; Sri Lanka made it national policy in 2021.
areas.whoPays: Farmers, through yields, and the poor, through food prices. Indian cotton farmers have revealed their preference.

figures.label: Sri Lanka: rice production in the six months after its 2021 fertiliser ban
figures.quote: rice production dropped 20 percent within six months of the ban, forcing Sri Lanka to import $450 million of rice

figures.label: Sri Lanka: rice production, 2021 to 2022
figures.quote: domestic rice production fell by 14% from 2021 to 2022
figures.notes: A different period from the six-month figure; both are kept.

figures.label: Indian cotton area under Bt (GM) cotton
figures.quote: ~96% of India's cotton area under Bt cotton (2023)

areas.against: Sri Lanka banned fertiliser overnight; a gradual shift with yield support is a different policy. Soil health, input debt and pesticide use are real costs of the chemical model, and GM mustard's opponents cite biosafety, not status.
areas.verdict: Where the policy was imposed, the poor paid; where farmers chose, they chose GM.

areas.belief: India must curb fossil-fuel growth now.
areas.whoHolds: Global climate advocacy and its supporters in India.
areas.whoPays: The answer here cuts the other way: the footprint is the elite's own.

figures.label: Emissions per person, richest 10% of Indians
figures.quote: The richest 10% of Indians emit roughly 10 tonnes per person a year, about what a European middle-class resident emits

figures.label: Richest 10%, another estimate (Bhattacharya 2020)
figures.quote: the top 10% emit about 8.8 tonnes

figures.label: Poorest 50% (Bhattacharya 2020)
figures.quote: The bottom 50% emit about 1 tonne on average

figures.label: Average Indian (Bhattacharya 2020)
figures.quote: The national average is 2.2 tCO2 per person

areas.against: The poorest 90% of Indians already have a footprint consistent with the 1.5°C goal (Climate Inequality Report 2023). A climate belief that targets the top 10%'s consumption is the opposite of a luxury belief; one that asks the poor to forgo electricity, gas cylinders or jobs in coal districts would be one. Which version is held matters more than the label.
areas.verdict: Not a luxury belief as such: the cost falls on the poor only if curbs land on their consumption rather than the rich's.

areas.whoHolds: Not obviously an elite belief: it is state policy, defended on behalf of poor households. It is listed because of who bears its costs.
areas.whoPays: Those who drink what the black market sells, and those it jails.

figures.label: Bihar total ban in force since
figures.quote: The state government imposed a total ban on sale and consumption of alcohol on April 5, 2016

figures.label: Deaths, Siwan and Saran hooch tragedy, October 2024
figures.quote: At least 25 people have died after consuming spurious liquor in the two districts
figures.notes: Later reports put the toll at 37 across Siwan, Saran and Gopalganj.

figures.label: Arrests in the ban's first four months, 2016
figures.quote: 4,707 people have been arrested in the last four months and 3,719 FIRs lodged for flouting the ban

areas.against: Its defenders argue that poor households gain from less drinking; no figure for that is cited here, and none for the costs either: no official cumulative death or arrest count has been published, and the opposition's "more than 1,300 deaths" is a political claim.
areas.verdict: A policy whose costs, and claimed benefits, fall on the poor — not a luxury belief in Henderson's sense.

areas.belief: Caste and community should not decide whom one marries.
areas.whoHolds: Liberal opinion, in what it says; the question is how far practice follows.
areas.whoPays: Couples who cross the line in places where it is enforced.

figures.label: Married women in inter-caste marriages (IHDS-II, 2011-12)
figures.quote: about 5.4% of married women aged 15 to 49 said their marriage was inter-caste, marginally higher for urban over rural India

figures.label: Hindus: very important to stop women marrying outside the religion
figures.quote: 67% of Hindus said it is very important to stop women in their community from marrying outside their religion

figures.label: Muslims: the same
figures.quote: Among Muslims, 80% said this about women

figures.label: Married Indians whose spouse shares their religion
figures.quote: Nearly all married people (99 percent) report that their spouse shares their religion

areas.against: The spouses' own schooling has no association with marrying across caste; the groom's mother's schooling does (IHDS analysis, Ideas for India). The "elite says one thing, does another" pattern is Henderson's charge, but the inter-caste rate barely differs between town and village; it hovers around 5% from 1970 to 2012.
areas.verdict: An almost universal practice of marrying within: the class gap is in what is said, not in what is done.

areas.belief: Violence against a wife is never justified.
areas.whoHolds: The better-off and better-schooled, more often — see the NFHS breakdown below.
areas.whoPays: Where the norm is weakest, women do.

figures.label: Women who say wife-beating is justified for some reason (NFHS-5)
figures.quote: 45% of women and 44% of men are okay with husbands beating wives
figures.notes: The DHS Program's NFHS-5 table for the same question, shown below, gives 38.2% of women and 33.5% of men. The two do not match, and which respondents the headline counts is not stated in the excerpt read.

figures.label: Men (NFHS-5)
figures.quote: 45% of women and 44% of men are okay with husbands beating wives
figures.notes: The DHS Program's NFHS-5 table for the same question, shown below, gives 38.2% of women and 33.5% of men. The two do not match, and which respondents the headline counts is not stated in the excerpt read.

areas.against: This is the case that shows the concept's limit: a belief held more by the better-off whose spread helps the poor is not a luxury belief, and the class gradient here runs in the poor's favour.
areas.verdict: Not a luxury belief: the elite norm protects the poor where it spreads.

areas.belief: Henderson's "defund the police" has no real Indian counterpart; the Indian question is whom the police serve.
areas.whoHolds: Across classes, Indians say the police treat rich and poor differently.

figures.label: Say police discriminate between rich and poor
figures.quote: Around 51 percent respondents believe police discriminate between rich and poor
figures.notes: Upper- and middle-class respondents were as likely to say so as the poor.

figures.label: Significant trust in a senior police officer
figures.quote: Only three in 10 people reported significant levels of trust in a senior police officer

figures.label: Satisfied with the police: Uttar Pradesh / Punjab
figures.quote: Himachal Pradesh and Haryana scored 71 per cent satisfaction, while UP scored 8 per cent and Punjab 9 per cent

areas.against: A belief shared across classes is, by definition, not a luxury belief; the US example does not travel.
areas.verdict: No class gap in belief to test.
